confirmed.issue: Segmentation of appositive structure is misleading - 'cell division' is labeled as subject (S) in parallel with main clause, but it is actually an appositive explaining 'one act'
confirmed.evidence: Text: 'That huge change happened through one act, repeated again and again: cell division, in which one cell splits into two.' The segmentation shows 'cell division,' as a new subject-verb clause, but grammatically it is an appositive noun phrase following the colon that clarifies what 'one act' means. The main clause has only one subject-verb pair: 'That huge change happened'.
confirmed.suggestion: Revise segmentation to show 'cell division, in which one cell splits into two' as an appositive phrase (APP) rather than as a separate S-V unit. This will correctly represent the sentence structure to students.

verdict.reason: The segmentation in sentence 2 of page3 incorrectly labels "cell division," as role S (subject), placing it in parallel with "That huge change" as if it were a coordinate subject. Grammatically, the sentence contains only one independent clause with a single subject-verb pair: "That huge change happened". The text "cell division" is an appositive noun phrase following the colon that clarifies/renames "one act" in the preceding prepositional phrase. The relative clause "in which one cell splits into two" modifies this appositive, but does not make "cell division" a sentence subject. The grammar note correctly identifies "콜론 + in which 관계절" (colon + relative clause), acknowledging the appositive structure, but the role assignment contradicts this analysis. This is a genuine annotation error: the role should reflect appositive status, not independent subject status.

minors.issue: Object and complement not cleanly separated in 'begin as' structure
minors.evidence: Segmentation lists O as 'your whole life as one tiny cell,' but grammatically 'your whole life' is the object and 'as one tiny cell' is an adverbial complement. The note mentions 'begin as' idiom but the O slot combines both. Compare to how other O+Complement structures are typically handled.
minors.suggestion: For clarity in teaching, consider separating: O='your whole life' and complement='as one tiny cell' in the segmentation, or explicitly label 'your whole life as one tiny cell' as O+Complement. This teaches more precise role distinction.
